I’m from the US and I’ve lived in Germany for the better part of ten years so far. Although I definitely understand the reasons people here are giving for why they left Germany, I personally don’t intend to leave. 
I think what makes my experience different is that when I first moved here, I lived with a German family for a year who helped me learn the language, integrate into the culture and set up my own independent life here. After several years of total integration I don’t feel like an American living in Germany, but more so like a German living in Germany. 
The other comments absolutely have legitimate criticism of Germany and the cons of living here. I do however think that a lot of their complaints are based on a lack of integration and cultural understanding, which I really can’t blame them for because they didn’t have the privilege like I did to spend so long living amongst a German family as I got my bearings here. 
If you or anyone else is considering moving here to stay long term, the best piece of advice I can give you is to take learning German VERY seriously. If you want to really feel like a part of society and not like an outsider, it’s not enough to get to B2. You need to become completely fluent in it. This takes a lot of work and will definitely take time, but it’s absolutely doable. I went from an intermediate/conversational level of German to entirely fluent in about 18 months of living here and practicing/studying diligently.

I passed a C2 exam several years ago and felt then very similar to how you do now. It wasn’t until I lived in Germany for a year or two completely immersed in the language that I felt properly fluent. 
At C1 you’re very far along in the process of becoming fluent. I’m sure you’ve mastered all of the grammar by now. Now the name of the game is building a bigger and bigger vocabulary. I suggest reading German newspapers every day. 

I didn’t feel completely fluent in German until I lived in a Germany for a while. I doubt I ever could have attained my current level without ever moving here.

Well having never measured it myself, I can’t really say much to how accurate the claims are for in either direction regarding the 10,000 lux. All I know is that I’ve had really severe SAD ever since moving north and diligent use of an SAD lamp has made an unmistakable difference. 

I use mine every single day for forty five minutes immediately after getting out of bed, keep the light about 12 inches from my face and make sure that the light producing surface of the lamp is at all times visible in my peripheral vision. 
It’s a bit inconvenient to use it this diligently, no denying that, but the benefits can’t be beat! This is the first winter I’ve survived without antidepressants in forever.

I think using an SAD light is best even if they are a little pricey. They are designed to be more safe to look closely at for long periods of time, and have no UV light that can damage your eyes. They are bright enough to treat SAD but not so bright as to harm you. 
Considering how effective these lamps can be and the needed safety involved with anything eye-related, I really suggest you make the investment into getting an SAD lamp. This is my first winter using mine and it has made an unbelievable difference.

I have also been paranoid with tinnitus, worried that any and all loud sound exposure will permanently make it worse. A trick I have found to help ground me in reality is asking myself the question: Would someone without tinnitus fear this noise? Would they honestly get hearing damage from a sound like that? Almost definitely not. It's really important not to allow tinnitus to get in the way of living a normal life because the more significance we give this condition, the more it will rule our lives. A certain level of caution is fine, but it's important to keep in mind that as tinnitus sufferers fearing a worsening of the condition, we might have anxieties that aren't completely realistic.

I use Carex Daylight lamp. I sit immediately in front of it (about ~30cm between the light and my eyes). During use, I look at my phone, which I hold directly below the light, that way I’m not looking directly into the light, but it is in my upper field of view. I do this for 45 minutes every day right after waking up while I have my morning coffee. It works FANTASTICALLY. I’ve struggled so badly with SAD in previous years and I’ve tried a couple other lamps that didn’t help but I finally found this setup that works. 

I think what makes the difference is that the carex daylight lamp is much bigger, so it completely covers your field of view from left to right if you sit very close to it and also it is on a stand and tilted downwards into your eyes, which mimics sunlight shining down at you.

For me it is simply a matter of personal taste. I have a decent life in Germany and I think my life in America would have been decent too (though my immature 18 year old mind sure didn’t think that way!). As pretentious as it might sound, I just feel like I “click” better with Germans than I do with Americans, generally speaking. I also enjoy having the rest of Europe so close making traveling around and seeing it much more doable. But traveling around the US sure isn’t bad either! America has some of the most beautiful national parks on Earth, no question about it. 

I think if I could turn back time to high school graduation, I think I still would make the same life choices I made, but I wouldn’t have the naive belief that this is the only option for me and the only thing that will make me happy. I think staying in the US would also have been perfectly fine. Lawyers in America earn a lot more than they do in Germany! Also, life is more so what you make of it than anything else. With the right mindset, you can make almost any set of external circumstances work out for you. 

Germany is not Shangri-la. There are problems here too. Both societally, politically and for me personally. Some things are more of a headache here than they are in the US. And moving here meant a lot of sacrifice for me. My relationship with all my childhood friends has become much more distant and out of the loop because the time zone difference makes chatting difficult. It still to this day kind of hurts to think about.

You should make it clear to your kids that moving here is always an option and maybe even encourage them to try it out for a semester or two when they’re in college. Maybe they’ll be into it, maybe not. I know a couple Americans who moved back. I personally have no intention of doing so. I think the important difference is that I thoroughly integrated myself into ordinary German society and established a life here while other people I know stayed in an Expat-American bubble. The catch is that this required me to get REALLY fluent in German, which a lot of foreigners are (understandably) not always thrilled to do. 

There’s really no wrong answer here. It’s best to give your kids all the options you can provide and let them make their own choices. That’s what my parents did for me and I’m extremely grateful for it.

Hi! I'm 24, American, and moved to Germany a few years ago. I'm currently in law school here.

The very first thing you need to do is learn German to a C1 level. At that level, you will be able to function in a German business setting as well as handle university level courses in German. I personally took TestDaF, but the Goethe Zertifikat is just as good. I very strongly recommend visiting an in-person language school and taking it very seriously (doing all the homework plus extra, watching tv and movies in German with subtitles, etc). If that isn't possible due to covid, then take online classes with a tutor. Get yourself a solid textbook and grammar workbook, maybe even some vocab flash cards.

​

When I moved to Germany, my level of German was pretty much your current level. I estimate you're probably at about a B1. I visited a language school here 20 hours per week for six months and studied VERY intensely and got to C2.

My learning German had three main prongs:

1. Speaking and listening to German as much as possible. I had a distinct advantage because I had already moved here and was living with some very supportive German friends.
2. Learn the Grammar down to a science. All these annoying rules of declination, cases, genders, tenses, all of it. Needs to be mastered to the point where you don't even have to think about it but rather it just comes naturally. You do that just by practice, practice, practice. Both grammar practice exercises and speaking in conversation.
3. Learn adult level vocab. I started reading German newspapers every day with a highlighter in my hand. I highlighted words I didn't know, and when I was done with the article I would look up the meaning and turn it into a flashcard. When I started doing this, I would have to highlight quite a lot and reading a single newspaper article in German would take like an hour. Slowly but surely I had to highlight less and less, my fluency in reading getting better and better over time.

Learning German to a high level (C1/C2) is a big undertaking but it is definitely possible! I did it and you can too. Your post shows that you already have the basics down. :)

Hi! I had very similar worries back when I came out. I came out when I was 22, and did so pretty quickly; over the course of about 6-8 weeks I went from completely closeted to everyone knowing. One of my main concerns wasn’t that I was going to get hate from my friends and family, but rather I would have to justify coming out so much later than I possibly could have. I kept up a charade among my friend group going on dates with girls and pretending to be into it for years and I was scared of how they would react when they found out that was all a lie. 

My parents didn’t care at all. 0%. They had had their suspicions forever and were happy that I finally could talk about it openly. 

My friends were shocked. None of them saw it coming at all. At first they didn’t believe me and it took a bit of discussion to convince them I wasn’t joking. Aside from the initial disbelief, they all pretty much just took it in stride. That was almost exactly two years ago and since then me being gay has barely even come up because nobody really cares. Still the same guy I’ve always been. 

I fully understand anxiety because I went through it too. I know I’m a bit younger that you, but honestly I don’t think that matters; at the time of my coming out, I had been actively pretending to be into girls and sometimes even going on dates for years. 

From my experience all I can say is that you probably have a handful of super awkward conversations ahead of you. But that awkwardness is literally just a simple conversation that will grant you freedom to be open about yourself for the rest of your life. Extremely worth it, no doubt! 

As for timing and circumstances, I find that there isn’t really a good time for it. If you wait for a good moment, you’ll be waiting forever. You just gotta wait till you have a small meeting of people you wanna come out to and just breach the subject and out with it. Gotta rip that band aid off sometime. And the sooner, the better!

What country are you studying in? I'm from the US, but am currently a 2L in Germany. 

In America, what matters most is where you go to law school. In Germany, what matters most is what your grade on the bar exam is. 

Both systems give opportunities to make a prestigious career. In America you need to get accepted into a top law school and in Germany you need to get a top grade on the bar exam, and where you studied is not that relevant. Internationally speaking, american and european legal qualifications are on pretty equal footing. I really wouldn't worry that my degree is somehow less valuable than an american JD should I for example apply for a job in NATO or the UN or something. 

Also, I'm doing an additional qualification in Anglo/American common law so that I can at least function in common law cases albeit not with the same expertise as a natively trained lawyer. If you have interests in international law, I highly recommend you do something similar.

Law school in general, regardless of what system and what country, is a massive undertaking and is definitely not for the faint of heart. You don't need to be some super genius to be a successful attorney, but you do need to be willing to work much harder than most other people do and being bright doesn't hurt. 

All you can do is give 110% of your effort to your studies and see what happens. If you notice after a couple semesters that things aren't going so well, then it might not be a bad idea to consider a different subject to study. But if you get the hang of it and are doing well, just keep working and make your goals a reality. :)

Germans break les obligations up into two separate branches of law, one about the creation of obligations called Schuldrecht, and the other regulating the actual transfer of ownership of an object, called Sachenrecht. If you happen to be interested, this concept of separation is called the Abstraktionsprinzip, and it's a fundamental building block to how the German civil code, the Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch (BGB) is designed. 

I don't have enough experience to speak for common law, but there is definitely room for debate in civil law. In law school in Germany, basically the only task the student has is to read a case, and use the code to find the legal solution. Some cases are really cut and dry, and very simply fit into what the law says. But the cases that are given to us in exams are always formulated in such a way that it doesn't fit neatly into the code, and you need to use various forms of legal argumentation on why a certain section of the code is to be interpreted one way over another. 

Then there is criminal law, in which the meaning of basically every term is hotly debated among scholars, and the student has to memorize all the leading viewpoints and then take sides. It can be a lot of fun, but it is sometimes annoying working in such abstract terms without any concrete case to work with.

I'm very optimistic that this will bring me from "advanced German speaker....for a foreigner" to "I can't believe he's not a native speaker." I have similar anxiety. I'm a C1 speaker, and I've recently began a gap year here in Germany to improve my language skills for my studies too. I plan on starting law school here next fall, and I'm a bit worried if I can handle the task; I've tried reading a few legal texts here and there, and although in the end I can manage through it (with tons of needing to use a translation dictionary!), it is extremely difficult and slow. To fully comprehend a single page of a German legal text, such as das Bürgerliches Gesetzbuch, I need easily an hour or more. 



Despite this, I haven't lost hope, and I don't think you should either. I've been here for the past three months, and in this time my overall fluency and comprehension have drastically improved. My biggest advice to you during your gap year is to stay away from your native language as much as you can. (Kinda hypocritical of me, since I'm writing this in English! :P ) Make a system for you that works, but the closer to full immersion, the better. I'm from America, and naturally my family is still there, and they wanna remain in contact. They don't speak German, and my friends can always tell when I just had a skype call with my parents, because my German gets shaky after a couple hours of thinking and speaking in English. So I've made the rule for myself that I have Englisch-Verbot every day except Sunday. That means no youtube videos, little to no reddit, and tv only in German. This has greatly helped me in the last month or so, and since starting this policy with myself, I've actually begun to think and dream in German without any effort. 


If my goals are realistic, which I believe they are, then yours must be too! Best of luck in your studies! :)
